questions.prompt: What does a stock's ticker symbol represent?
choices: A short code that uniquely identifies a company's stock, like AAPL for Apple
The company's total yearly profit
The number of shares you personally own
The dividend the company pays
questions.explanation: A ticker is just a nickname code exchanges use to identify a stock quickly. AAPL means Apple, TSLA means Tesla.

questions.prompt: A stock's share price alone tells you how big the company is.
questions.explanation: Price is per share. A $500 stock can be a smaller company than a $20 stock. Company size is measured by market cap, not price.

questions.prompt: A company has 10,000,000 shares priced at $50 each. What is its market cap, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Market cap = share price x shares outstanding. $50 x 10,000,000 = $500,000,000.

questions.prompt: What does market capitalization (market cap) measure?
choices: The total value of all a company's shares: share price x shares outstanding
The price of a single share
How many employees a company has
The company's yearly advertising budget
questions.explanation: Market cap adds up every share's value, so it reflects the company's true size far better than the price of one share.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a stock quote to what it tells you.
pairs: How much the price moved today
Total value of all the shares
questions.explanation: Each field answers a different question: what it is, how it moved, how big the company is, and how actively it's trading.

questions.prompt: A stock opened at $200 and now trades at $210. What is its percent change today?
Which of these can you read straight from a stock quote? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: The current share price
Today's percent change
The market cap
Exactly what the price will be tomorrow
questions.explanation: A quote shows today's price, move, and company size. No quote can tell you tomorrow's price.

questions.prompt: What is a market order?
choices: An order to buy or sell right away at the best price currently available
An order that only fills at a price you choose
A promise to hold a stock for one year
A fee charged by the exchange
questions.explanation: A market order says 'fill me now, whatever the going price is.' You get speed, but not a guaranteed price.

questions.prompt: What is a limit order?
choices: An order that only executes at your chosen price or better
An order that fills instantly at any price
An order to sell your entire portfolio
A type of savings account
questions.explanation: A limit order says 'only fill me at my price or better.' You control the price, but it might never fill.

questions.prompt: A market order prioritizes speed, while a limit order prioritizes price control.
questions.explanation: That's the core trade-off: market = fast but price uncertain; limit = price certain but the fill isn't guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Highest price a buyer will pay
Lowest price a seller will accept
questions.explanation: Buyers post bids, sellers post asks, and your order type decides whether you chase speed or hold out for a price.

questions.prompt: Sort each situation into the order type that fits best.
items: Buy right now, the exact price doesn't matter much
Only buy if it drops to $50
Sell instantly to exit a falling stock
Sell only if it climbs to $100
questions.explanation: Use a market order when getting in or out fast matters most, and a limit order when hitting a specific price matters most.

questions.prompt: A limit order guarantees your order will always be filled.
questions.explanation: A limit order guarantees the price, not the fill. If the stock never reaches your price, the order simply waits or expires.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of placing a limit buy order in order.
items: Submit and wait for the price to reach it
questions.explanation: You choose the stock, pick 'limit,' set your price ceiling, then let it sit until the market comes to your price.

questions.prompt: What is a bull market?
choices: A stretch when prices are generally rising and optimism is high
A stretch when prices are generally falling
A single day of heavy trading
A tax on stock gains
questions.explanation: Picture a bull charging with its horns up. A bull market is a rising, optimistic market.

questions.prompt: What is a bear market?
choices: A stretch when prices fall 20% or more from recent highs
A stretch when prices keep hitting new highs
A market that only trades bonds
A market with zero price movement
questions.explanation: Picture a bear swiping its paw down. A bear market is a falling market, officially a drop of 20% or more.

questions.prompt: A market is officially a 'bear market' once it falls at least what percent from its recent high?
questions.explanation: The widely used rule of thumb is a 20% drop from the recent peak.

questions.prompt: An index peaks at 5,000 and falls to 4,000. What percent has it dropped?
questions.explanation: (5,000 - 4,000) / 5,000 = 0.20 = 20% — exactly the bear-market threshold.

questions.prompt: The smartest move in a bear market is always to panic-sell everything.
questions.explanation: Panic-selling locks in losses. Historically, markets have recovered over time, so staying calm and sticking to a plan usually beats panicking.

questions.prompt: Match each market term to its meaning.
pairs: A drop of about 10% from highs
How much prices swing up and down
questions.explanation: A correction is a milder dip than a bear market, and volatility just describes how jumpy prices are.

questions.prompt: Which are smart habits during a bear market? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Stay calm and stick to your long-term plan
Keep investing steadily if you can
Sell everything the moment prices dip
Remember markets have recovered from past crashes
questions.explanation: Calm, consistency, and perspective help. Reflexively selling on every dip is what turns temporary drops into permanent losses.

questions.prompt: What is a call option?
choices: The right to BUY a stock at a set price before a deadline
The right to SELL a stock at a set price
A guaranteed dividend payment
A loan from your broker
questions.explanation: Call = the right to Call the stock toward you (buy it) at a fixed price. Calls are a bullish bet.

questions.prompt: What is a put option?
choices: The right to SELL a stock at a set price before a deadline
The right to BUY a stock at a set price
A type of index fund
A savings bond
questions.explanation: Put = the right to Put the stock away from you (sell it) at a fixed price. Puts are a bearish bet.

questions.prompt: One standard options contract controls 100 shares of the stock.
questions.explanation: Almost all equity options come in bundles of 100 shares per contract, so small price moves get magnified.

questions.prompt: You buy 2 call contracts. How many shares do they control in total?
questions.explanation: Each contract is 100 shares, so 2 contracts control 2 x 100 = 200 shares.

questions.prompt: What is the 'premium' on an option?
choices: The price you pay to buy the option
The profit you're guaranteed to make
A special tax on options
The number of shares in one contract
questions.explanation: The premium is the cost of the option itself — the money you hand over to hold that right.

questions.prompt: Sort each idea into the view it expresses.
items: You think the stock will rise
You think the stock will fall
questions.explanation: Calls profit when the stock climbs (bullish); puts profit when it drops (bearish).

questions.prompt: When you BUY an option, the most you can lose is the premium you paid.
questions.explanation: If the bet goes wrong, the option can expire worthless — but you can never lose more than the premium you spent to buy it.

questions.prompt: You're bullish on a stock — you expect its price to climb. Which option matches that view?
choices: Buy a call
Buy a put
Sell all your shares immediately
Options can't express this view
questions.explanation: Bullish means you expect a rise, and a call profits as the stock goes up. Call = bullish.

questions.prompt: Build the position that fits Toro's view.
questions.scenario: You're convinced NVDA will jump after its earnings report next week.
questions.success: A call profits when the stock climbs above your strike plus the premium you paid.
questions.explanation: A bullish view calls for a call. It locks in the right to buy NVDA at $150 even if the stock rockets past it.

questions.prompt: You're bearish on a stock — you expect its price to drop. Which option matches that view?
choices: Buy a put
Buy a call
Buy more shares
Options can't express this view
questions.explanation: Bearish means you expect a fall, and a put profits as the stock goes down. Put = bearish.

questions.prompt: Build the position that fits Toro's view.
questions.scenario: You think TSLA will slide after weak delivery numbers come out.
questions.success: A put profits when the stock falls below your strike minus the premium paid.
questions.explanation: A bearish view calls for a put. It locks in the right to sell TSLA at $230 even if the stock sinks far below.

questions.prompt: A call costs a $3.00 premium per share. Since 1 contract covers 100 shares, what does 1 contract cost in total, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Premium is quoted per share, so $3.00 x 100 shares = $300 for one contract.

questions.prompt: Build the position that fits Toro's view.
questions.scenario: You expect AAPL to rally into the holiday shopping season.
questions.success: A call profits when the stock climbs above your strike plus the premium you paid.
questions.explanation: Expecting a rise is bullish, so you buy a call — the right to buy AAPL at $230 no matter how high it goes.

questions.prompt: If you buy that call for a $300 premium, the most you can lose is $300.
questions.explanation: When you buy an option, your entire risk is the premium. Worst case, it expires worthless and you're out $300 — no more.

questions.prompt: What is a ticker symbol?
choices: A short code that identifies a company's stock
The total number of shares outstanding
A company's yearly revenue
The exchange's opening time
questions.explanation: A ticker like AAPL or NVDA is just a quick ID code for a stock.

questions.prompt: A company has 20,000,000 shares priced at $30 each. What is its market cap, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Market cap = price x shares. $30 x 20,000,000 = $600,000,000.

questions.prompt: A market order is best described as...
choices: Buy or sell immediately at the best available price
Buy or sell only at a price you set
A plan to hold a stock for ten years
An order that can never be cancelled
questions.explanation: Market orders trade speed for price certainty — they fill right away at whatever price is available.

questions.prompt: A limit order guarantees your price, but not that the order will fill.
questions.explanation: If the stock never reaches your limit price, the order simply doesn't execute.

questions.prompt: A stock rises from $200 to $250. What is its percent change?
By the common definition, a market becomes a 'bear market' after it falls at least...
choices: 20% from its recent high
5% from its recent high
50% from its recent high
1% in a single day
questions.explanation: A 20% drop from the recent peak is the standard bear-market line.

questions.prompt: A call option gives you the right to...
choices: BUY a stock at a set price
SELL a stock at a set price
Collect a guaranteed dividend
Borrow shares for free
questions.explanation: Calls are the right to buy and are a bullish bet; puts are the right to sell and are bearish.

questions.prompt: When you buy an option, the most you can lose is the premium you paid.
questions.explanation: The premium is your entire risk when buying an option — it can expire worthless, but you can't lose more than you spent.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Executes at your price or better
The right to SELL at a set price
questions.explanation: These four span the whole unit: market mood, order types, options, and company size.

questions.prompt: Sort each idea into the market view it expresses.
questions.explanation: Calls and rising-price expectations are bullish; puts and falling-price fears are bearish.
